The Night Watch was commissioned around 1639 as a group portrait of Amsterdam’s civic militia guards, completed by Rembrandt in 1642.
It was made for one of the three headquarters of Amsterdam's civic guard, groups of civilian soldiers who defended the city from attack.
Rembrandt was the first to depict all figures in action rather than in a static pose, showing the militia company moving out under Captain Frans Banninck Cocq.
The painting’s nickname, The Night Watch, is a misnomer that arose later because it was mistakenly thought to depict a nocturnal scene.
In 2013, the painting was restored and ceremoniously transported through Amsterdam in a custom-made box, celebrated by thousands of people, marking its return to the Rijksmuseum.
Currently, the Rijksmuseum is conducting "Operation Night Watch," a public restoration project removing old varnish with microscopic precision to preserve the painting for future generations.
'Het Joodse bruidje', ook bekend als 'Isaak en Rebekka', is een schilderij van Rembrandt uit circa 1665-1669, dat sinds 1885 in bruikleen is van de gemeente Amsterdam aan het Rijksmuseum.
Het werk toont een intieme omhelzing tussen een man en een vrouw, waarbij Rembrandt oorspronkelijk een derde figuur had gepland, maar deze weggelaten heeft om de focus op het paar te leggen.

Het schilderij was van 1833 tot 1854 eigendom van de bankier Adriaan van der Hoop, die zijn collectie aan Amsterdam naliet onder de voorwaarde dat deze intact en toegankelijk bleef; dankzij particuliere steun kon de stad de successierechten betalen en kwam het werk uiteindelijk in het Rijksmuseum.
Rembrandt wilde met dit late werk niet zozeer actie tonen, maar de innerlijke gevoelens en zieleroerselen van het paar, wat hij uitdrukte via het licht en het expressieve materiaalgebruik.

De titel 'Het Joodse bruidje' is niet van Rembrandt zelf, maar verwijst vermoedelijk naar het Bijbelse echtpaar Isaak en Rebekka, wat wordt ondersteund door een voorstudie waarop een derde man te zien is die het paar bespiedt, een detail dat op het uiteindelijke schilderij ontbreekt.
View of Houses in Delft, also known as The Little Street, was painted by Johannes Vermeer around 1658 and depicts ordinary houses in Delft, including the home of Vermeer’s aunt Ariaentgen Claes.
The painting was gifted to the Rijksmuseum by H.W.A.
Deterding, London.
The work is unusual for Vermeer as it focuses on a simple street scene rather than a wide cityscape or notable event, showing a tranquil glimpse of daily life in 17th-century Delft.
Vermeer originally painted a woman sitting by the doorpost on the right but later removed her to enhance the sense of depth in the composition.

The painting’s provenance includes ownership by Pieter Claesz van Ruijven and his family, followed by several collectors before eventually entering the Rijksmuseum collection through Deterding’s donation.
The Great Wave off Kanagawa was created by Katsushika Hokusai in late 1831 during the Edo period as part of his series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji.
The print captures a moment of intense natural power, showing three boats struggling against a towering, cresting wave with Mount Fuji in the background.
Hokusai used Prussian blue pigment, which was a new and revolutionary color in Japanese prints at the time, contributing to the print's striking visual impact.
The composition combines traditional Japanese ukiyo-e techniques with European graphical perspective, reflecting cross-cultural influences.
The Great Wave became immediately successful in Japan and later influenced European Impressionists.
Several museums worldwide, including the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, hold original prints that often came from 19th-century private collections of Japanese prints.
The Milkmaid was painted by Johannes Vermeer around 1657–1661, with the Rijksmuseum estimating circa 1658 as the date of completion.
Vermeer chose to depict a simple domestic kitchen maid absorbed in the everyday task of pouring milk, elevating a humble moment into a subject of artistic focus.
The painting is noted for its striking illusionism and the way Vermeer captured the weight and texture of objects and the figure, shaping the style for which he is known.
The work was acquired by the Dutch state for the Rijksmuseum after a 1907 controversy over whether it should be sold to a wealthy American collector.
Vermeer’s technique involved careful observation of light playing over surfaces, using hundreds of colorful dots to achieve this effect.

Emanuel Leutze’s painting *Washington Crossing the Delaware* was completed in Germany seventy-five years after the actual event and is now housed at The Met Fifth Avenue.
The painting depicts the moment before the Battle of Trenton on December 26, 1776, a turning point in the American Revolutionary War.
The work was donated to The Met by Mrs.
Mary E.
Kennedy in 1911, significantly enhancing the museum’s American art collection.
Kennedy’s donation changed the museum’s holdings by adding a large-scale, iconic image of American patriotism and leadership.
The painting symbolizes unity with its thirteen figures representing the original colonies, including James Monroe holding the flag, foreshadowing his future presidency.
Leutze’s depiction was inspired more by European riverscapes than the actual icy Delaware River conditions.
The Musicians was commissioned by Cardinal Francesco Maria del Monte, who had a strong interest in music and owned expensive musical instruments that Caravaggio could use as models.
Caravaggio entered del Monte’s household around 1595, and The Musicians is believed to be his first painting made expressly for the Cardinal.
This commission played a significant role in supporting Caravaggio’s early career by immersing him in aristocratic musical culture, which influenced his artistic development.
The painting features four figures likely painted from life, reflecting del Monte’s patronage and taste.
After Cardinal del Monte’s death, the painting was sold on May 8 (year not fully provided).
The Death of Socrates was painted by Jacques-Louis David in 1787 as part of the neoclassical style popular in the 1780s, depicting the story of Socrates' execution as told by Plato in his Phaedo.
The painting shows Socrates calmly accepting death by poison hemlock after being convicted of corrupting the youth and introducing strange gods, using his death as a final lesson rather than fleeing.

David’s portrayal emphasizes Socrates’ philosophical commitment to living and dying according to his principles, highlighting that Socrates was remembered primarily for his philosophical life and how he faced death.

The use of color in the painting, with vibrant reds near the center and bluish-white on Socrates and Plato, serves to underscore the emotional intensity and calm serenity of Socrates and his disciple.
This work reflects the idea that philosophy is not just theoretical but a way of life, with Socrates as a role model for living and dying with integrity.

The Harvesters is an oil painting on wood completed by Pieter Bruegel the Elder in 1565 and measures approximately 119 by 162 centimeters.
It was commissioned by Nicolaes Jonghelinck, a merchant banker and art collector from Antwerp, as part of a cycle of six paintings depicting different times of the year.
The painting shows peasants harvesting wheat and engaging in activities such as eating and cock throwing, reflecting 16th-century rural Belgian life without religious themes.
The Harvesters has been at The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City since 1919, acquired through the Rogers Fund.
This work is considered a “watershed in the history of Western art” and is called the “first modern landscape” by the museum.
